Chapter 9: The Ongoing Struggle with Visibility
Living in a large body is complicated, isn’t it? On one hand, you can’t help but stand out in a crowd—people stare, they whisper, you feel their eyes on you. But on the other hand, there’s a strange sort of invisibility too. People look right past you. They ignore your needs, sometimes even act like you’re not there at all.
That push and pull—of being both seen and unseen—shapes daily life in ways most folks don’t realize. Maybe you’ve been in a meeting where your ideas just float by unnoticed, or you get overlooked for a promotion. At a party, you’re the last one greeted, and somehow the first to be forgotten. Even in the doctor’s office, your pain might be minimized, your concerns brushed aside. The message you get is pretty clear: you’re somehow both too much, and not enough, all at once.
Living with that double-edged visibility can bring a lot of anxiety. Every time you leave the house, you’re running through calculations—will this chair hold me? Are the stares going to be cruel today? Will I be safe? The world’s gaze is relentless, and it takes real strength just to keep showing up. To keep insisting, “I have the right to exist here.”
But you know what? There are moments of defiance, too. Like the woman who finally got tired of apologizing for her size. She decided to wear that bright, beautiful dress. She took up space. She laughed out loud, not caring who was watching. Sure, the stares came. But so did a brand new sense of freedom. It turns out, visibility can be a kind of power—a way to claim your place in a world that keeps telling you to shrink.
Most people have no idea how much courage it takes to be visible. To refuse to fade into the background. But every single act of showing up, of letting yourself be seen, is a step closer to a world where all bodies are truly welcome.
